identity.title: Benchmarking pre-main sequence stellar evolutionary tracks using disk-based dynamical stellar masses

paper_type_evidence.quote: The parent sample comprises 37 disks in the Upper Scorpius region from (cite: Carpenter2025), for which (cite: Zallio_2026) measured dynamical stellar masses modeling ALMA Band 7 $^{12}$CO $J = 3-2$ visibilities.
The disk-based dynamical masses were taken from (cite: Zallio_2026).

question.value: Compare disk-based dynamical stellar masses with pre-main sequence evolutionary model predictions on the HR diagram to benchmark their predictive power and underlying physics.

evidence.quote: In this work we compare stellar masses derived from protoplanetary disk rotation, i.e. “dynamical” masses independent of stellar evolutionary models, with stellar masses predicted by modern PMS evolutionary models using observed effective temperatures and luminosities.
This comparison provides a direct benchmark of their predictive power and the relevance of their underlying physics.

analysis_steps.goal: Compare dynamical masses and HR diagram masses across evolutionary models

method.value: Compute the percentage of sources agreeing within 1-sigma (quadratic sum of uncertainties), the median mass ratio <R> = <M_star,dyn / M_star,HRD> for sources in 0.1 < M_star < 1.3 M_sun, and Spearman rank correlation coefficients between relative mass discrepancy and dynamical mass.

evidence.quote: In addition to the fraction of sources in agreement, we quantify the typical offset between dynamically-derived stellar masses and theoretical track-inferred stellar masses by computing the median mass ratio: $\langle R \rangle = \langle M_{\star,\text{dyn}} / M_{\star,\text{HRD}} \rangle$

To ensure a fair comparison among the models, we report the percentage of agreement and the median mass ratio $\langle R \rangle$ only for sources with a defined mass value in all evolutionary models (i.e., within the mass range $0.1 < M_\star < 1.3 \> M_\odot$).

To assess whether the mass discrepancies exhibit a stellar-mass dependence, we computed Spearman rank correlation coefficients between $(M_{\star,\rm{HRD}} - M_{\star,\rm{dyn}})/M_{\star,\rm{dyn}}$ and $M_{\star,\rm{dyn}}$.

key_parameters.value: Mass range 0.1 < M_star < 1.3 M_sun; agreement threshold +/- 1 sigma

evidence.quote: To ensure a fair comparison among the models, we report the percentage of agreement and the median mass ratio $\langle R \rangle$ only for sources with a defined mass value in all evolutionary models (i.e., within the mass range $0.1 < M_\star < 1.3 \> M_\odot$).

Figs. 1 and 2 show that the best match with dynamical stellar masses is provided by the SPOTS pre-main sequence tracks with $f=17\%$ cold spot coverage ($100\%$ agreement within $\pm1\sigma$, where $\sigma$ is the quadratic sum of the model and dynamical mass uncertainties)

validation.value: Evaluated fraction of sources in agreement and <R> including upper and lower limits, confirming results remain unchanged apart from minor variations.

evidence.quote: We also evaluated the fraction of sources with consistent mass estimates and $\langle R \rangle$ including upper and lower limits, and found that, apart from minor variations, the results remain unchanged.

results_numeric.quantity: Reduction in age scatter across evolutionary tracks when using dynamical mass prior

evidence.quote: Finally, in Fig. 7, we show that when a prior on the stellar mass is considered for HR diagram fitting, the median inferred ages across different tracks become much more consistent, and the scatter among different evolutionary tracks reduces from $3.4$ Myr to $0.8$ Myr, an improvement $\gtrsim77\%$.

findings_qualitative.value: SPOTS evolutionary tracks with f=17% cold spot coverage best reproduce dynamical stellar masses in the 0.1-1.3 M_sun range.

evidence.quote: The SPOTS evolutionary tracks of (cite: Somers_2020) with $f=17\%$ best reproduce ($100\%$ agreement within $\pm1\sigma$ uncertainties) the dynamical stellar masses in the stellar range $0.1-1.3$ $M_{\odot}$.

findings_qualitative.value: Most evolutionary models show no statistically significant stellar-mass dependence in their mass discrepancies, except PARSEC v2.0 and SPOTS models with f >= 51% which show a negative correlation.

evidence.quote: Most models show no statistically significant correlation ($p>0.05$), but PARSEC v2.0 and SPOTS models with $f\geq51\%$ display a negative correlation (Spearman coefficient $\rho\leq-0.77$, with $p<10^{-3}$), implying a significant mass-dependent bias.

findings_qualitative.value: Incorporating dynamical stellar mass priors into HR diagram fitting greatly reduces age-mass degeneracy and makes median inferred ages across different evolutionary tracks much more consistent.

evidence.loc: The impact of stellar mass priors on the age of single objects
evidence.quote: When including a gaussian mass prior based on the dynamical mass and its associated uncertainty, the age-mass degeneracy reduces greatly, as shown in Fig. 5 (right).

When using stellar dynamical masses as mass priors for HR diagram fitting, the median inferred ages across different tracks become consistent, and the scatter decreases by $\gtrsim77\%$, while individual ages can vary by up to $\sim25\%$.

claims.hypothesis: Modern pre-main sequence evolutionary tracks accurately predict stellar masses of young stars in the 0.1-1.3 M_sun range when compared to model-independent disk-based dynamical masses.
claims.experiment: Compare ALMA 12CO J=3-2 visibility-derived dynamical stellar masses (with simulation-calibrated uncertainties) against HR diagram masses derived using ysoisochrone for 10 PMS evolutionary track grids on 20 Upper Scorpius sources.
claims.result: SPOTS tracks with f=17% spot coverage achieve 100% agreement within 1-sigma; non-magnetic tracks (Baraffe+15, Feiden+16 non-magnetic, Siess+2000, SPOTS f=0%) underestimate masses by 10-26%, while magnetic (Feiden+16 magnetic), PARSEC v2.0, and higher spot coverage tracks (SPOTS f=34%, 51%, 85%) overestimate masses by 20-32%.
claims.finding: SPOTS evolutionary tracks with a moderate 17% cold spot coverage best reproduce the dynamical stellar masses in the 0.1-1.3 M_sun range, lying between non-magnetic and magnetic Feiden (2016) predictions.

evidence.quote: Figs. 1 and 2 show that the best match with dynamical stellar masses is provided by the SPOTS pre-main sequence tracks with $f=17\%$ cold spot coverage ($100\%$ agreement within $\pm1\sigma$, where $\sigma$ is the quadratic sum of the model and dynamical mass uncertainties)

On average, the HR diagram masses derived using the magnetic tracks of (cite: Feiden2016), PARSEC v2.0 ((cite: Nguyen_2022)), and SPOTS ((cite: Somers_2020)) with $f=34\%$, $51\%$, $85 \%$ overestimate the dynamical masses by $\sim20\%$, $\sim21\%$, $\sim20\%$, $\sim27\%$, $\sim32\%$, respectively.

Those provided by the tracks of (cite: Baraffe2015), (cite: Feiden2016) non-magnetic, (cite: Siess_2000) and SPOTS with $f=0\%$ underestimate them by $\sim15\%$, $\sim12\%$, $\sim26\%$, $\sim10\%$, respectively.

claims.hypothesis: Discrepancies between HR diagram-derived masses and dynamical masses exhibit a systematic dependence on stellar mass.
claims.experiment: Compute Spearman rank correlation coefficients between (M_star,HRD - M_star,dyn)/M_star,dyn and M_star,dyn for each evolutionary model.
claims.result: Most evolutionary models have p > 0.05, whereas PARSEC v2.0 and SPOTS models with f >= 51% show Spearman coefficient rho <= -0.77 with p < 10^-3.
claims.finding: Most models show no statistically significant stellar-mass dependence, except PARSEC v2.0 and high spot fraction (f >= 51%) SPOTS models which exhibit a significant negative mass-dependent bias.

evidence.quote: To assess whether the mass discrepancies exhibit a stellar-mass dependence, we computed Spearman rank correlation coefficients between $(M_{\star,\rm{HRD}} - M_{\star,\rm{dyn}})/M_{\star,\rm{dyn}}$ and $M_{\star,\rm{dyn}}$.

Most models show no statistically significant correlation ($p>0.05$), but PARSEC v2.0 and SPOTS models with $f\geq51\%$ display a negative correlation (Spearman coefficient $\rho\leq-0.77$, with $p<10^{-3}$), implying a significant mass-dependent bias.

claims.hypothesis: Incorporating disk-based dynamical stellar masses as priors in HR diagram fitting improves age consistency across different PMS evolutionary models.
claims.experiment: Perform Bayesian HR diagram fitting with ysoisochrone across all 10 evolutionary tracks with and without Gaussian priors set by the dynamical masses and their uncertainties.
claims.result: Single-source median ages shift by ~25% (for SPOTS f=17%), and across the 10 evolutionary tracks the median age shifts from ~6.5 Myr to ~6.8 Myr while inter-track scatter drops from 3.4 Myr to 0.8 Myr (>=77% improvement).
claims.finding: Using dynamical stellar masses as priors reduces age-mass degeneracy and forces inferred ages across different evolutionary models to converge to a consistent median age.

evidence.quote: Finally, in Fig. 7, we show that when a prior on the stellar mass is considered for HR diagram fitting, the median inferred ages across different tracks become much more consistent, and the scatter among different evolutionary tracks reduces from $3.4$ Myr to $0.8$ Myr, an improvement $\gtrsim77\%$.

When using stellar dynamical masses as mass priors for HR diagram fitting, the median inferred ages across different tracks become consistent, and the scatter decreases by $\gtrsim77\%$, while individual ages can vary by up to $\sim25\%$.

why_this_data.value: Targets in Upper Scorpius were selected because they have accurate ALMA dynamical masses from 12CO rotation, precise Gaia parallaxes (varpi/sigma > 10), and broad-band flux-calibrated VLT/X-Shooter spectra that allow reliable modeling of veiling, extinction, and spectral type.

evidence.quote: The targets were selected based on the availability of accurate dynamical masses, reliable stellar parameters, and precise *Gaia* parallaxes ($\varpi/\sigma(\varpi)>10$).

These spectra are well-suited for young stars because they allow a better modeling of veiling, extinction, and spectral type for the targets (e.g., (cite: Herczeg_2014; Manara_2013; Manara_2020; Manara_2023)).

why_this_method.value: Because statistical uncertainties on dynamical masses from parametric visibility fitting in Zallio et al. (2026) are unrealistically small, a grid of mcfost + csalt simulations was used to evaluate and assign conservative mean statistical uncertainties.

evidence.loc: Uncertainties on the dynamical mass measurements due to inclination, stellar mass, and disk size
evidence.quote: Since the stellar mass statistical uncertainties reported by (cite: Zallio_2026) are systematically underestimated due to limitations of fitting visibilities with parametric models, we decide to test the accuracy of the `csalt` dynamical mass measurements by creating and fitting a grid of numerical simulations.

evidence.loc: Uncertainties on the dynamical mass measurements due to inclination, stellar mass, and disk size
evidence.quote: This choice is motivated by the fact that the mean statistical uncertainties are found to be greater than the systematic uncertainty, and we therefore opt for a conservative approach.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Including upper and lower mass limits when computing the fraction of consistent sources and median mass ratio <R> (tested and found to leave results unchanged apart from minor variations).

evidence.quote: We also evaluated the fraction of sources with consistent mass estimates and $\langle R \rangle$ including upper and lower limits, and found that, apart from minor variations, the results remain unchanged.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Modeling deviations from Keplerian motion due to pressure gradients and disk self-gravity (not considered because angular and spectral resolution are insufficient to detect them).

evidence.quote: However, due to the limited angular ($0.1-0.3^{\prime\prime}$) and spectral ($\sim480$ ms$^{-1}$) resolution of the data presented in (cite: Carpenter2025), we emphasize that such deviations remain undetectable, and were therefore not considered in the analysis.

limitations_admitted.value: Assumption of purely Keplerian rotation neglects pressure gradients and disk self-gravity, which can alter inferred central masses by 5-10%.

evidence.quote: One limitation of our analysis lies in the assumption of purely Keplerian rotation (including the dependence on the disk’s vertical height) within protoplanetary disks.

For instance, (cite: Andrews_2024) and (cite: Longarini_2025) demonstrated that deviations from Keplerian motion induced by pressure support can alter the inferred mass of the central object by as much as $5-10\%$.

limitations_admitted.value: Limited angular (0.1-0.3 arcsec) and spectral (~480 m s^-1) resolution of the ALMA observations.

evidence.quote: However, due to the limited angular ($0.1-0.3^{\prime\prime}$) and spectral ($\sim480$ ms$^{-1}$) resolution of the data presented in (cite: Carpenter2025), we emphasize that such deviations remain undetectable, and were therefore not considered in the analysis.

limitations_admitted.value: Comparison is restricted to the age of Upper Scorpius (4-14 Myr), and whether agreement holds at younger ages remains to be tested.

evidence.quote: Since evolutionary models have a strong time-dependent aspect, our comparison demonstrates the consistency of disk-based stellar masses with HR diagram predictions at the age of Upper Scorpius ($4-14$ Myr, (cite: Ratzenbock_2023a; Ratzenbock_2023b)).
Whether this agreement holds at different ages remains to be tested, and will be explored, for example, with the DEC/O Large Program for the younger ages.

limitations_admitted.value: In the simulation grid, csalt fits at disk inclination of 55 deg show a discrepancy of ~10% in the worst case.

evidence.loc: Uncertainties on the dynamical mass measurements due to inclination, stellar mass, and disk size
evidence.quote: Most of our fits return results in agreement with the true stellar mass, except for the sources with inc $=55$°, as shown in Fig. 3, where the discrepancy is $\sim10\%$ in the worst case.

referee_caveats_inferred: The stellar parameters (Teff, L*) come from an unpublished work in preparation (Empey et al., in prep.) and are not tabulated in the main text, making independent verification of the HRD fitting dependent on the external repository.
The 100% agreement for SPOTS f=17% depends directly on the inflated dynamical mass uncertainties assigned via the coarse 3x3 simulation grid in Table 1.
Cold spot coverage is assumed constant across the entire 0.1-1.3 M_sun mass range, whereas spot properties may vary with stellar mass or magnetic activity.
